knowledge_requirements.description: Recognition of severe external bleeding, immediate bleeding-control measures, bystander limitations, and emergency medical escalation.
Recognition of an unresponsive person, immediate safety actions, responsiveness/breathing assessment where supported, recovery positioning where appropriate, and emergency escalation.
Recognition of serious breathing difficulty, immediate bystander actions, choking/airway emergencies where supported, and emergency medical escalation.
Immediate first aid for thermal burns, cooling, unsafe substances or actions to avoid, and criteria requiring urgent medical care.
Recognition of suspected fractures, immediate precautions, immobilization/support principles, actions to avoid, and emergency escalation.
Recognition of potentially serious head injury, warning signs, immediate precautions, movement considerations, and emergency escalation.
Situations suggesting spinal injury, safe handling, minimizing unnecessary movement, trained-responder involvement, and emergency escalation.
Recognition of shock, immediate supportive first-aid actions, actions to avoid, and emergency medical escalation.
Protecting a person during a seizure, preventing secondary injury, actions that should not be performed, post-seizure care where supported, and criteria for emergency medical assistance.

Added because roadside collapse due to heat exposure is a highly plausible Indian roadside scenario given climate conditions. Covers recognition of heat exhaustion vs. heatstroke, immediate cooling actions, and emergency escalation.

knowledge_records.scenario: A person is bleeding heavily from a wound after a roadside injury.
knowledge_records.answer: Apply firm, direct pressure on the wound using a clean cloth or dressing and keep pressing continuously. If possible and no fracture is suspected, raise the injured part above the level of the heart. Keep the person lying down and still, reassure them, and call for emergency medical help. If the dressing soaks through, add more layers on top rather than removing it. Watch for signs of shock while waiting for help.
key_actions: Ensure your own safety before approaching
Apply firm direct pressure on the wound with a clean cloth/dressing
Raise the injured limb above heart level if no fracture is suspected
Keep the person lying down and still
Call emergency medical services
Continue to monitor for shock while waiting for help
do_not: Do not remove the original dressing if it becomes soaked; add more on top
Do not leave the bleeding person unattended
escalation_criteria: Bleeding does not stop with sustained direct pressure
Wound is deep, large, or gaping
Signs of shock appear (pale, cold, clammy skin, rapid weak pulse)
knowledge_records.notes: Based on NHS (UK) severe bleeding first-aid guidance. No India-specific authoritative source with equivalent procedural detail was verified in this research pass; see GAP-001.

knowledge_records.scenario: There is an object (e.g., glass, metal) embedded in a wound and the area is bleeding.
knowledge_records.answer: Do not remove an embedded object, as it may be helping to control the bleeding. Apply pressure around the object rather than directly on it, and build up padding on either side to stabilize it without pressing it further in. Call emergency medical services immediately.
key_actions: Do not remove the embedded object
Apply pressure around, not on, the object
Build padding around the object to stabilize it
Call emergency medical services
do_not: Do not remove or push on the embedded object
Do not apply direct pressure on top of the object
escalation_criteria: Any embedded object with active bleeding requires emergency medical response
knowledge_records.notes: Based on NHS (UK) severe bleeding guidance. International source; India-specific equivalent not verified (GAP-001).

knowledge_records.topic: Checking an unresponsive person and recovery position
knowledge_records.scenario: A person is not responding after an accident or collapse.
knowledge_records.answer: Check responsiveness by talking loudly and gently shaking the shoulders. Shout for help. Check if the person is breathing normally. If they are breathing normally, place them in the recovery position (on their side, head tilted back slightly to keep the airway open) and call emergency services. Stay with them and monitor breathing continuously until help arrives. If they are not breathing normally or show no signs of life, call emergency services immediately.
key_actions: Ensure scene safety before approaching
Check responsiveness (talk loudly, gently shake shoulders)
Shout for help
Check for normal breathing
If breathing normally, place in the recovery position
Call emergency medical services
Continuously monitor breathing until help arrives
do_not: Do not leave an unconscious breathing person lying flat on their back unattended
Do not give the person anything to eat or drink
escalation_criteria: Person is not breathing normally or shows no signs of life
Person does not regain responsiveness
knowledge_records.notes: Based on NHS (UK) 'unconscious person' and 'recovery position' guidance. If trauma/spinal injury is suspected, cross-reference KR-007 (REC-010) before repositioning; this is a potential procedural tension flagged in human_review context via GAP notes.

knowledge_records.topic: Hands-only CPR by an untrained bystander
knowledge_records.scenario: A person is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
knowledge_records.answer: If a person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services immediately. An untrained bystander can perform hands-only CPR: push hard and fast in the center of the chest with minimal interruption until professional help arrives, an automated external defibrillator (AED) becomes available, or the person begins to breathe normally.
key_actions: Call emergency services immediately
Begin chest compressions in the center of the chest
Push hard and fast with minimal interruption
Continue until professional help arrives or person breathes normally
do_not: Do not delay calling emergency services to attempt first aid
Do not attempt rescue breaths without training if unsure of technique
escalation_criteria: Any unresponsive person not breathing normally is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate emergency services contact
knowledge_records.notes: Based on American Heart Association hands-only CPR public guidance, designed specifically for untrained bystanders. This is a US-based professional medical organization; no equivalent India-specific lay-CPR public guidance (e.g., Indian Resuscitation Council) was verified in this pass (see GAP-004). Do not present AHA guidance as Indian official protocol.

knowledge_records.scenario: A person is choking and cannot breathe, cough, or speak.
knowledge_records.answer: If the person can cough forcefully, encourage them to keep coughing. If they cannot cough, speak, or breathe, give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades. If this does not clear the obstruction, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts. Alternate between back blows and abdominal thrusts. Call emergency services if the obstruction does not clear.
key_actions: Encourage forceful coughing if the person can still cough
Give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts if back blows do not work
Alternate back blows and abdominal thrusts
Call emergency services if the obstruction persists
do_not: Do not perform blind finger sweeps of the mouth
Do not interrupt a person who is coughing forcefully on their own
escalation_criteria: Obstruction does not clear after repeated cycles of back blows and abdominal thrusts
Person becomes unconscious
knowledge_records.notes: Based on NHS (UK) adult choking guidance. If person becomes unconscious, this escalates to KR-002 (REC-003/REC-004) procedures.

knowledge_records.topic: Severe breathing difficulty (non-choking, e.g., asthma-type attack)
knowledge_records.scenario: A person is having serious trouble breathing but is not choking on an object.
knowledge_records.answer: Help the person sit upright in a comfortable position; do not lay them down. Stay calm and reassure them, and loosen any tight clothing. If they have their own reliever inhaler, help them use it. Call emergency services if breathing does not improve, if their lips or face turn blue, if they cannot speak in full sentences, or if they become drowsy or exhausted.
key_actions: Help the person sit upright, not lying down
Loosen tight clothing
Help them use their own reliever inhaler if they have one
Stay calm and reassure the person
Call emergency services if there is no improvement or warning signs appear
do_not: Do not lay the person flat
Do not give a bystander's own medication to the person
escalation_criteria: No improvement in breathing
Blue lips or face
Cannot speak in full sentences
Becoming drowsy or exhausted
knowledge_records.notes: Based on NHS (UK) asthma attack first-aid guidance, used here as the closest verified authoritative analogue for general severe breathing difficulty. Other causes of breathing difficulty (e.g., anaphylaxis, chest trauma) are not covered — see GAP-005.

knowledge_records.scenario: A person has a burn from heat, fire, or a hot surface.
knowledge_records.answer: Cool the burn under cool (not iced) running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible. Remove clothing or jewelry near the burnt area before it swells, unless it is stuck to the skin. Cover the burn loosely with cling film or a clean, non-fluffy material. Keep the person warm to avoid hypothermia while cooling the burn. Seek emergency medical care for large or deep burns, or burns on the face, hands, feet, genitals, or major joints.
key_actions: Ensure safety and stop the burning process
Cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes
Remove nearby clothing/jewelry before swelling occurs (if not stuck to skin)
Cover loosely with cling film or clean non-fluffy material
Keep the person warm elsewhere on the body
Seek emergency medical care for serious burns
do_not: Do not use ice or iced water
Do not apply butter, oil, ointments, or toothpaste
Do not burst blisters
Do not use fluffy materials like cotton wool on the burn
Do not remove clothing that is stuck to the burn
escalation_criteria: Burn larger than the person's hand
Deep burns of any size
Burns on the face, hands, feet, genitals, or major joints
Chemical or electrical burns
Signs of shock
knowledge_records.notes: Based on NHS (UK) burns and scalds first-aid guidance. No India-specific authoritative burns first-aid public guidance was verified (see GAP-001).

knowledge_records.scenario: A person may have a broken bone after a fall or collision.
knowledge_records.answer: Encourage the person to keep still and avoid moving the injured part. Support the limb in the position it was found, using padding or your hands, without trying to straighten or realign it. If there is an open wound, cover it with a clean dressing. Call for emergency medical help, especially for suspected fractures of the thigh, hip, pelvis, spine, or skull.
key_actions: Keep the person still and calm
Support the injured limb in the position found
Cover any open wound with a clean dressing
Avoid unnecessary movement of the injured area
Call emergency medical services for suspected serious fractures
do_not: Do not try to realign or straighten the bone
Do not move the person unnecessarily
Do not let the person eat or drink in case surgery is needed
escalation_criteria: Bone visible through the skin (open fracture)
Heavy bleeding
Deformity with loss of pulse or sensation below the injury
Suspected fracture of spine, hip, pelvis, or skull
knowledge_records.notes: Based on NHS (UK) broken bone first-aid guidance. No India-specific equivalent verified (see GAP-001).

knowledge_records.topic: Warning signs after a head injury
knowledge_records.scenario: A person has hit their head, for example in a fall or road accident.
knowledge_records.answer: Most minor bumps to the head are not serious, but watch closely for warning signs: loss of consciousness, confusion or drowsiness that does not improve, repeated vomiting, a seizure, clear fluid leaking from the nose or ears, difficulty speaking, weakness in the limbs, unequal pupil size, or a severe or worsening headache. Keep the person still, monitor them closely, and seek emergency medical attention immediately if any of these signs appear or if the injury followed a high-impact event.
key_actions: Keep the person still and monitor them
Watch for warning signs listed above
Seek emergency medical attention immediately if any warning sign appears
Seek medical attention for any head injury following a high-impact event (e.g., road accident, fall from height)
do_not: Do not assume a head injury is minor without monitoring for warning signs
Do not let the person resume normal activity if warning signs are present
escalation_criteria: Loss of consciousness
Persistent confusion or drowsiness
Repeated vomiting
Seizure
Fluid leaking from nose/ears
Unequal pupils
Severe or worsening headache
knowledge_records.notes: Based on NHS (UK) head injury/concussion guidance. Motorcycle-helmet-specific handling in head/spinal injury (highly relevant to Indian roadside two-wheeler accidents) is NOT covered by this source — see GAP-008.

knowledge_records.scenario: A person may have a spinal injury after a fall or road collision.
knowledge_records.answer: Suspect a spinal injury if a person has a painful neck or back injury after a significant fall or collision, complains of numbness, tingling, or weakness in the limbs, or is found unconscious after trauma. If the person is not in immediate danger, do not move them. Keep the head, neck, and back as still as possible, support the head with hands on either side if needed, reassure the person to stay still, and call emergency services so trained responders can safely manage movement and extrication. Only move the person if they are in immediate danger, such as fire or oncoming traffic.
key_actions: Assess for signs suggesting spinal injury
Keep the person as still as possible if not in immediate danger
Support the head and neck without forcing movement
Reassure the person to remain still
Call emergency services for trained responders
do_not: Do not attempt to sit the person up
Do not twist or bend the neck or back
Do not remove a motorcycle helmet unless absolutely necessary for airway/breathing (specific technique not verified — see GAP-008)
escalation_criteria: Any suspected spinal injury requires emergency medical response
Immediate danger (fire, traffic, unstable structure) may require careful movement despite suspected spinal injury
knowledge_records.notes: Based on St John Ambulance (UK) spinal injury first-aid guidance, recalled with moderate confidence; the exact live URL/content should be re-verified before ingestion (see GAP-007). This is a Critical requirement with weaker source confidence than other records — flagged in source_coverage_matrix as Insufficient and in human_review context.

knowledge_records.topic: Recognizing and helping someone in shock
knowledge_records.scenario: A person appears pale, cold, and weak after an injury.
knowledge_records.answer: Signs of shock include pale or grey, cold, clammy skin; rapid, shallow breathing; a rapid, weak pulse; nausea; and confusion or drowsiness. Lay the person down if possible, and raise and support their legs unless a leg injury, spinal injury, or fracture is suspected. Keep them warm with a blanket, do not give them anything to eat or drink, reassure them, and call emergency services immediately, since shock usually indicates a serious underlying injury.
key_actions: Recognize signs of shock
Lay the person down
Raise and support the legs if no leg/spinal injury or fracture is suspected
Keep the person warm
Call emergency medical services
Reassure and monitor the person until help arrives
do_not: Do not give the person food or drink
Do not raise the legs if a leg fracture or spinal injury is suspected
escalation_criteria: Any recognized signs of shock require immediate emergency medical services contact
knowledge_records.notes: Based on NHS (UK) shock first-aid guidance. No India-specific equivalent verified (see GAP-001).

knowledge_records.topic: Helping someone during and after a seizure
knowledge_records.scenario: A person is having a seizure (fit) at the roadside.
knowledge_records.answer: Protect the person from injury by clearing away hazardous objects or furniture, and cushion their head with something soft. Do not hold them down or restrain their movements, and do not put anything in their mouth. Note the time the seizure starts. Once the jerking stops, check their breathing and place them in the recovery position, staying with them and talking calmly as they regain awareness.
key_actions: Clear the area of hazards
Cushion the person's head
Time the seizure
After jerking stops, check breathing and place in recovery position
Stay with the person and reassure them as they recover
do_not: Do not restrain the person's movements
Do not put anything in the person's mouth
escalation_criteria: Seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes
Repeated seizures without regaining consciousness between them
It is the person's first known seizure
The person is injured during the seizure
Difficulty breathing after the seizure ends
The seizure occurred in water or a dangerous location
knowledge_records.notes: Based on NHS (UK) seizure first-aid guidance. No India-specific equivalent verified (see GAP-001).

knowledge_records.scenario: A person appears to be collapsing or unwell from heat exposure at the roadside.
knowledge_records.answer: Move the person to a cool place, remove unnecessary clothing, and cool their skin using cool water, a cool wet cloth, or fanning. If they are fully conscious, encourage them to sip a cool drink. Stay with them until they feel better. Heatstroke is a medical emergency — signs include very high body temperature, hot skin that is not sweating, a fast heartbeat, fast breathing, confusion, seizure, or loss of consciousness. If these signs are present, call emergency medical services immediately while continuing to cool the person.
key_actions: Move the person to a cool place
Remove unnecessary clothing
Cool the skin with water, a cool cloth, or fanning
Give a cool drink if the person is fully conscious
Call emergency services immediately if heatstroke signs are present, and continue cooling while waiting
do_not: Do not give fluids to a person who is not fully conscious
Do not wait to see if symptoms improve if heatstroke signs (e.g., seizure, loss of consciousness, hot skin not sweating) are present
escalation_criteria: No improvement after about 30 minutes of active cooling
Very high body temperature with hot, dry skin
Confusion, seizure, or loss of consciousness
knowledge_records.notes: Based on NHS (UK) heat exhaustion/heatstroke guidance. Highly relevant to Indian climate/roadside conditions, but no India-specific bystander first-aid source (e.g., NDMA heat action plan bystander instructions) was verified in this pass — see GAP-006.

knowledge_gaps.topic: Motorcycle helmet removal in suspected head/spinal injury
knowledge_gaps.missing_information: No authoritative source was verified for whether/how a bystander should handle a motorcycle helmet on an injured rider with suspected head or spinal injury — a very common Indian roadside scenario given high two-wheeler usage. This is a significant, unresolved practical gap.

General unconsciousness guidance (REC-003) recommends the recovery position for a breathing unconscious person, while spinal injury guidance (REC-010) recommends minimizing movement. Authoritative sources generally note that airway/breathing takes priority over spinal precautions, but this was not explicitly cross-verified between the two specific cited sources in this pass.
